analysis.one_liner: Let people see, correct, and control genetic records the government keeps on them.
analysis.headline: The Human Genome Privacy Act died without a vote: referred to two House committees and three subcommittees, it drew zero cosponsors and no action before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given people enforceable rights over genetic information held by federal agencies and their contractors: the right to see and copy their records for free, correct errors, and require written, purpose-specific consent before most disclosures. It backed those rights with criminal fines and a private right to sue, with minimum damages of $1,000. It arrived just as federal funding for the Human Genome Project was ramping up, when lawmakers worried genetic data could be used against people in jobs, insurance, and credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals whose genetic information is held by federal agencies or by contractors and grantees doing federally funded genetic research. They would gain free access to their records, the right to fix errors, control over who receives their data, and the ability to sue and collect damages when agencies or employees knowingly or negligently violated those rights [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals the right to inspect and get a free copy of any genetic information a government agency keeps about them, with a 10-day deadline for the agency to respond and an offer to explain the results.
Lets people correct or supplement wrong genetic records within 45 days, and if the agency refuses, attach a written statement of disagreement that travels with any future disclosure.

Bars agencies from disclosing genetic information without a signed, written authorization that names the recipient and the specific purpose, so data collected for one use could not quietly flow to another.

Extends the same protections to genetic information held by federal contractors and grantees, covering the researchers funded by the hundreds of millions of dollars Congress was appropriating for the Human Genome Project.

Puts teeth in the rights: criminal fines up to $10,000 for willful improper disclosure and up to $30,000 for selling stolen genetic data, plus a civil suit with minimum $1,000 damages and attorney fees for knowing or negligent violations.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies, and the contractors and grantees that maintain genetic data for them, bear the cost: building access and correction procedures, drafting notices of information practices, honoring consent limits before disclosures, and facing civil damages and criminal fines when they violate the rules [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill left large law-enforcement doors open: agencies could hand genetic information to police without any authorization to identify or locate a suspect or fugitive based on a supervisor's written certification, and courts could delay telling the person that their records were taken, with gag orders on the agency.

It covered only government agencies and their contractors and grantees, not the private employers, insurers, and lenders that the bill's own findings said were the real danger from genetic misuse, so the main threat Congress identified went unaddressed.

Agencies would face real administrative costs to set up inspection, amendment, notice, and consent-tracking systems, and the minimum $1,000 civil damages provision could invite litigation over ordinary record-keeping mistakes.
Penalty ceilings were modest — $10,000 for most willful violations — which an honest supporter would acknowledge may not have deterred a determined violator.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections were genuine and inexpensive relative to the stakes of a growing federal genetic-data enterprise, and the bill retained sensible exceptions for treatment, emergencies, and courts. But it was a half-measure even on its own terms: it shielded government databases while leaving private employers and insurers — the misuse channels its findings flagged — untouched, and its law-enforcement exceptions with delayed notice significantly diluted the privacy promise.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then three subcommittees, none of which ever held a hearing or voted, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the Human Genome Privacy Act on September 13, 1990, late in the second session of the 101st Congress.
The bill was referred jointly to the House Government Operations and Judiciary Committees on the day it was introduced.

Over the next three weeks it was routed to three subcommittees — Legislation and National Security and Government Information, Justice and Agriculture on September 18, then Civil and Constitutional Rights on October 2 — and none took further action.
The bill drew no cosponsors from either party.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in the record before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and their contractors and grantees came out ahead: they continue to maintain and share genetic records without individual access, correction, or consent rights, and without exposure to the bill's fines and lawsuits. No one gained the privacy protections.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Human Genome Privacy Act on September 13, 1990; no colleagues joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Government Operations Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to two subcommittees, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A lone Democratic sponsor attracted zero cosponsors from either party and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan pattern shows up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have forced agencies to give individuals access and correction rights, obtain written consent before most disclosures, and risk $10,000 fines and civil suits. Law enforcement, treatment, and emergency exceptions kept much of their internal use intact, but their discretion over Americans' genetic data would have been sharply limited.

industries.industry: Federally funded genome research contractors and grantees
industries.note: Contractors and grantees maintaining genetic information under federal contracts — including Human Genome Project work funded at roughly $150 million a year by 1991 — would have been treated like agencies, bound by the same access, consent, and penalty rules. Their interest in collecting and analyzing genetic data freely ran against the individual privacy rights the bill created.
